content.title: About
content.content: Breadsticks are dry, crunchy wheat‑flour products baked to a golden crust. This version is hard in texture and has reduced sodium (2453 mg per 100 g), making it more suitable for people monitoring their salt intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The hard texture is achieved by longer baking at low humidity.
Sodium reduction is done by replacing part of the salt with herbs and spices.
Breadsticks are a traditional Mediterranean snack served with dips and cheeses.
In Italy a similar product is called “grissini” and is often served with olive oil.
The sturdy shape makes them convenient for long‑term storage without losing crispness.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower sodium helps maintain normal blood pressure for individuals limiting salt consumption.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides a slow release of energy, contributing to prolonged satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: In modest amounts, breadsticks supply fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: The hard texture makes them ideal as a base for canapés, cheese plates, and dips, expanding dietary options.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Breadsticks contain wheat, so they are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Despite reduced sodium, the product remains calorie‑dense; portion control is important for weight management.

items.title: Hard texture
items.content: Young children and individuals with chewing difficulties may find these sticks hard to eat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breadsticks can be enjoyed as a snack on their own, served with olive oil, hummus, cheese spreads, or used as a crunchy base for canapés. For extra aroma, lightly warm them in the oven before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness. Discard any sticks showing mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Cauliflower is an edible cruciferous vegetable obtained after boiling, steaming or roasting. Cooked cauliflower has a tender texture, a mild flavor, and retains most of its nutrients, including vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, and dietary fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The white color of cauliflower florets gives it its name, though purple, orange and green varieties also exist.
In Japan it is often processed into "rice"‑like granules as a low‑carb alternative.
Cauliflower is rich in glucosinolates, which convert during cooking into compounds with anti‑cancer properties.
In ancient Roman cuisine it was sometimes referred to as "Brussels cabbage," a term now used for a different vegetable.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Cooked cauliflower is low‑calorie, making it a good choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Glucosinolates and carotenoids help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cauliflower.

items.title: Thyroid concerns
items.content: Large amounts of raw cauliflower can affect thyroid function due to goitrogens; cooking reduces this effect.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Some individuals may experience increased gas or abdominal discomfort after eating cauliflower.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked cauliflower can be served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, salads, mashed, or used as a "rice" substitute. It pairs well with olive oil, garlic, lemon, and a variety of herbs and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cauliflower in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags after cooling.

content.title: About
content.content: Light roasted coffee in a bottle or can is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from carefully selected light‑roasted coffee beans. The coffee is usually filtered, diluted with water and sealed in airtight packaging, preserving aroma and freshness without any brewing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Light roasting retains more acidity and fruity notes than dark roasting.
Bottled coffee first appeared in Japan in the 1970s as a convenient cold‑coffee option.
Most brands use cold‑brew extraction, which reduces bitterness and creates a smoother taste.
Aluminum or glass containers protect the drink from light, extending shelf life.
Light coffee often contains slightly less caffeine than dark because of the shorter roast time.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Light roasting preserves chlorogenic acid, a powerful antioxidant that helps combat free radicals.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Caffeine can increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, enhancing alertness and reaction time.

items.title: Reduced risk of certain diseases
items.content: Moderate regular coffee consumption is linked to lower risk of Parkinson’s disease and type 2 diabetes.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Unlike hot coffee, a cold ready‑to‑drink provides a notable contribution to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored versions often contain added sugars, increasing calorie count.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain stimulants and diminish the efficacy of sedatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chill the bottle and enjoy straight from it or pour over ice. Add a slice of lemon, mint, or a splash of milk to soften the flavor if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dark place. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days. Do not leave the bottle open at room temperature for more than a day.

cream-puff-eclair-custard-or-cream-fille.title: Cream Puff / Eclair (filled with custard or cream, no icing)

content.title: About
content.content: A cream puff or eclair is a light choux pastry filled with custard, pastry cream or whipped cream and served without icing (NS). The dough is made from water, butter, flour and eggs, while the filling can be vanilla, chocolate, fruit or nut flavored.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The eclair originated in France in the 19th century.
The name “eclair” means “lightning” in French, because it is meant to be eaten quickly.
Cream puffs are often sold as individual desserts or in mini‑boxes for catering.
A glaze‑free version keeps the pastry light and lets the filling shine.
Common fillings include pastry cream, custard, fruit mousse and almond cream.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides carbohydrates from the dough and fats from butter for a quick energy boost.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: If the filling is dairy‑based, it supplies calcium and vitamin D important for bone health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Eggs in the dough and cream add a modest amount of protein for tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The pastry contains B1, B2 and B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Sweet treats can trigger endorphin release, improving mood.

items.title: Dairy or egg allergy
items.content: The creamy filling often contains milk and eggs, which may cause reactions in allergic individuals.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: Overconsumption can contribute to weight gain and blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: One eclair can contain 150–250 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans‑fat risk
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter in the dough may introduce trans fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cream puffs at room temperature. They can be eaten whole, split open and topped with fresh berries, fruit sauce, or a dusting of powdered sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Let stand at room temperature for 15–20 minutes before serving to soften the pastry.

content.title: About
content.content: The Double Cheeseburger from McDonalds is a classic fast‑food sandwich made of two beef patties, two slices of Cheddar cheese, pickles, onions, mustard and ketchup, all sandwiched between a soft sesame‑seed bun. The item has been on the menu for over 20 years and is one of the most popular cheese‑lover choices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Double Cheeseburger was introduced in the United States in the early 1990s as an extension of the original cheeseburger.
In Russia the product is often simply called “double cheeseburger” without the brand name, though it is officially sold only in McDonalds restaurants.
Each patty weighs about 45 g, giving the whole burger a total weight of roughly 200 g.
The recipe may vary slightly between countries due to local regulations and taste preferences.
The burger is served in McDonalds’ signature cardboard wrapper, which is easily recyclable.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Two beef patties provide about 20 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheddar cheese adds calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is rich in B12 and B6 vitamins, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates provides quick, sustained energy.

items.title: High calories and saturated fat
items.content: One Double Cheeseburger contains roughly 450–500 kcal and over 20 g of saturated fat, which can contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ketchup, mustard and pickles make the sandwich fairly salty (≈900 mg sodium), which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product contains milk, gluten (bun) and soy (in some sauces), which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: In some markets the patties include preservatives and flavor enhancers that may be undesirable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten hot, holding the bottom bun to avoid burning your hands. It pairs well with fries, a dipping sauce, or a soft drink. For a healthier twist, add fresh lettuce, tomato or other vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Freshly prepared burgers should be consumed immediately. If you need to store them, wrap tightly in foil and keep refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a microwave or oven to restore bun crispness.

sausage-noodles-and-vegetables-excluding.title: Sausage, noodles and vegetables without carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens, tomato‑based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: This dish combines boiled or fried sausage pieces, cooked noodles and a mix of vegetables (such as bell pepper, zucchini, peas) simmered in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce. It is quick to prepare, hearty, and works well for lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tomato sauce is often made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic and basil.
Noodles absorb the sauce’s aroma, making the dish richer in flavor.
Sausage adds protein and a distinctive taste, but can be swapped for chicken or turkey for a lighter version.
Excluding carrots, broccoli and leafy greens gives a milder taste while still providing essential nutrients from the remaining vegetables.
The meal is popular in fast family dinners and school cafeterias because of its simplicity.

items.title: Protein from sausage
items.content: Sausage supplies essential amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Carbohydrates from noodles
items.content: Noodles provide quickly digestible carbs, delivering energy for an active day.

items.title: Vitamins from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables like bell pepper and zucchini are rich in vitamin C and potassium, supporting immunity and fluid balance.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant linked to reduced risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain noodles (if used) add fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Sodium and fat in sausage
items.content: Processed sausages are often high in salt and saturated fat; people with hypertension should choose lean options or use less.

items.title: Allergy to spices
items.content: Tomato sauce may contain garlic, onion or spices that can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some ready‑made sauces contain added MSG, which can cause headaches in susceptible people.

items.title: Processed meat concerns
items.content: Frequent consumption of processed meats is associated with higher risk of certain diseases; moderation is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs (such as parsley) and grated cheese if desired. A dash of hot sauce or a drizzle of olive oil can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat with a splash of water or broth to keep the sauce from drying out.
